newsitem.title: USA: Ex-U.S. Navy analyst gets prison term for spying.
newsitem.headline: Ex-U.S. Navy analyst gets prison term for spying.

text.p: A federal judge on Friday sentenced former U.S. Navy intelligence analyst Robert Kim to nine years in prison for passing classified documents to a South Korean military official in 1996.

U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema rejected a plea of leniency by a tearful, Bible-quoting Kim, who had been a civilian computer specialist for 19 years at the Office of Naval Intelligence until his arrest on espionage charges.
Brinkema handed down the tough sentence, saying the Korean-born Kim had betrayed the public's trust to safeguard secrets and the oath of loyalty to the United States when he became a citizen in 1974.
She rejected his arguments that he had been naive and had been a victim, manipulated by the official at the South Korean embassy, Navy Capt. Baek Dong-Il, to whom he had passed the documents.
"You knew what you were doing," Brinkema said, as the 57-year-old Kim stood before her in a courtroom packed with family members and friends.

She acknowledged that it represented a tragic day for Kim and his family, but expressed concern about the message that would be sent if he got a a lenient sentence. Under the law, Kim faced a maximum of 10 years in prison.

The judge said Kim would get credit for the 9-1/2 months he already has spent in jail since his arrest by the FBI at a diplomatic reception at Fort Myer, Virginia. She also placed him on probation for three years.
While addressing the judge, Kim started crying when he said he had missed his youngest daughter's graduation from the University of Virginia and would be unable to attend his son's wedding.

He quoted several passages from the Bible, expressing sorrow for his "horrible mistake" and saying he had repented and that God had forgiven him. Kim asked the judge to impose "appropriate and reasonable" punishment so he could be reunited with his family as soon as possible.
Although he pleaded guilty in May to conspiring to commit espionage, he still maintained, "I am not a spy. I am not a foreign agent for South Korea."
Defence attorneys portrayed Kim as a model citizen, without even a parking ticket, before his arrest and said he made numerous contributions to the community and his church.

But Brinkema rejected those arguments, saying he had been entrusted with the highest government security clearance. And noting he had considered passing documents at his church, "I think that is horrible hypocrisy," she said.
Prosecutor Robert Chesnut urged the judge to reject the pleas of leniency made on Kim's behalf by family, church members and even South Korean government officials.
"He was looking to cash in on what he had learned at the Office of Naval Intelligence," he said. "He put his love for another country ahead of his responsibility."

Chesnut said Kim had been reluctant to cooperate with U.S. officials in telling them about his espionage activities, claiming not to remember and holding back some information until the day before sentencing.
